name: Pedro Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Pedro, thanks for talking with me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, what's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Normal day, I'm underground. I run a loader at a gold mine, the long low machine that scoops the broken rock after a blast and carries it to the ore pass, the shaft where it drops down to be crushed. We go down in the cage at six, do the pre-start checks, and then it's mucking, that's what we call clearing the rock, for most of the shift on level 14. I've been doing it about eighteen months, so I still get the easy headings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good part is the crew. Old Rafa trains me and he talks the whole time, about football, his grandkids, which rock is going to fall. The hard part is the heat and the dust, and the money is less than people think when you're on the trainee rate. Ana, my girlfriend, works in an aged care home, and between us we cover rent and not a lot else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, to my brother mostly, because he's been sending me videos about robots taking everything. At work I'd say nothing changes, back to the face. Online maybe a joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd be relieved, but I'd still want the union to keep an eye on things. Some of this stuff is already here without big AI, like the remote loaders on level 9 that a guy runs from a chair on the surface. So it's not nothing, it's just slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep learning the loader properly so I get off the easy headings. Ana and I talked about putting a little away for a car, so I'd start that, maybe thirty a fortnight. And I'd keep paying union dues, I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly calm. A bit boring, which is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the remote loaders on level 9. Have you tried one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once. Rafa got me ten minutes in the chair during a shift change. It's like a video game with a lag, and you feel the rock less, you can't hear it. I wasn't good at it but I wasn't terrible either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your brother sends you robot videos. What does he think you should do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks I should get out and do something with computers, but he works in a phone shop, so that's his whole world. I tell him gold doesn't come out of a phone. We argue about it every Sunday at our mother's.

S0.say: I'd say to my brother and my crew that nothing really changed and it's back to the face. Online I'd maybe make a joke about all the robot hype.
S0.think: I think I'd be relieved, but the union should still watch the remote loaders that already run from the surface. It's not nothing, it's just slow.
S0.do: Keeps working and gets better on the loader so he moves off the easy headings. Starts saving about thirty a fortnight with his girlfriend for a car and keeps paying union dues.
S0.feel: Mostly calm, a little bored, which he says is good.
S0.quote: It's like a video game with a lag, and you feel the rock less, you can't hear it.
S0.fieldNote: He's relaxed in this picture but alert to the remote loaders already working on another level. He's had ten minutes in the remote chair and wasn't put off by it. The Sunday arguments with his brother show the tech question is already part of family life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when the union earns its money. If the company is going to change how we work, we get a say in how, and we get trained on the company's time. I'd put that on the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job changes rather than disappears, at least for a while. Someone has to run the remote loaders, and someone has to fix them. But I'm junior and still slow, so I'm worried I'm not the someone they pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the tele-remote training the first time they offer it, and I'd ask Rafa to put a word in. I'd use one of those AI chat apps to help me understand the manuals, I already do that sometimes for forms. And we'd stop the car savings and put it into rent backup instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but like before a test you could pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the union should get a say. What would that look like on your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A list. Who gets trained first, by seniority and by who wants it, not just whoever the shift boss likes. And no one gets moved off the loaders without six months notice. That's not crazy, other sites have that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you got the remote job and Rafa didn't, how would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. He taught me everything. He'd say good on you, kid, and then he'd go quiet at lunch. I'd want the union to find him something, maybe teaching the new ones safety, because nobody knows the ground like him.

S1.say: I'd say this is when the union earns its money and that workers should have a say and be trained on company time. I'd post that in the union group chat.
S1.think: I think my job changes rather than disappears for a while, because someone has to run and fix the remote loaders. I'm worried a slow junior like me won't be the one they pick.
S1.do: Signs up for tele-remote training the first time it's offered and asks his trainer to put in a word. Uses an AI chat app to understand the manuals and moves the car savings into a rent backup.
S1.feel: Nervous, like before a test he could pass.
S1.quote: Someone has to run the remote loaders, and someone has to fix them. But I'm junior and still slow, so I'm worried I'm not the someone they pick.
S1.fieldNote: He wants both: a fair union process and to be first in line for the remote job. The thought of beating his trainer to it clearly bothers him. He reaches for AI tools practically, as a reading aid rather than something he's excited about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster for working people and the government has to step in now, with money, not speeches. I'd go to the protests, and I'd tell my brother he was right, which would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means even the remote chair is gone, because the machine won't need me in the chair. I've got secondary school, a loader ticket and eighteen months. That's nothing in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd talk to Ana about whose job lasts longer, and I think hers does, people want a human with their grandmother. So I'd take any shifts I could get while the mine still needs people and we'd save everything. If it all goes, I'd sign up for whatever support scheme exists and probably go back to my mother's house in the town, me and Ana in my old room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd be lying if I said anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You think aged care lasts longer. Even with robots doing hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope so. I don't know. Ana says the residents scream at the robot vacuum, so maybe. But if it's cheaper, the company that owns her home doesn't care who screams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone plan and anything with a subscription, then eating out, which is just the chicken place on Fridays anyway. Rent we can't cut unless we move, so moving is really the first big thing.

S2.say: I'd say it's a disaster for working people and the government has to step in now with money, not speeches. I'd go to protests and admit to my brother he was right.
S2.think: I think two years means even the remote chair is gone because the machine won't need a person. With secondary school and eighteen months on a loader, I'd have nothing to offer.
S2.do: Takes every shift he can while the mine still needs people and saves everything with his girlfriend. If the job goes, signs up for support schemes and moves into his mother's house with her.
S2.quote: The machine won't need me in the chair.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture removes the stepping stone he'd counted on in the slower one. He leans on his partner's job lasting longer, while admitting he doesn't really know. His instinct is to save hard and fall back on family, with protest as a public outlet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's use them, with a plan from government and the company for towns like ours. I'd want the union pushing for a transition fund, money set aside to help people move into new work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to get one thing under my belt. Maybe the remote ticket, maybe something else. But I also think the thing I learn could be gone by the end of it, so I'd have to pick carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the older guys and the other sites do for the first year, then jump on whatever's working. Probably the remote ticket, and an electrical course at the technical college at night, because things still break and robots need fixing. And I'd keep the rent backup going, maybe fifty a fortnight now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but busy, which is better than worried and doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a year rather than start straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen guys jump at things that went nowhere. A guy on my crew paid for a drone course and the mine bought drones and gave the job to the surveyors. I'd rather go second and go right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say about you doing night classes after shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say yes and then complain I'm never home, and she'd be right. We'd probably fight about it once, then make it work. She did her care certificate while working nights, so she can't say much.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years and should use them, with a plan from government and the company for mining towns. I'd want the union pushing for a transition fund to help people into new work.
S3.think: I think five years is enough to get one thing under my belt, but what I learn could be gone by the end. I'd have to pick carefully.
S3.do: Watches what other workers and sites do for about a year, then commits to the remote operator ticket and a night electrical course. Raises the rent backup to about fifty a fortnight.
S3.feel: Worried but busy, which he prefers to worrying and doing nothing.
S3.quote: I'd rather go second and go right.
S3.fieldNote: This captures his steady style well: he waits to see what works before committing, citing a colleague who wasted money on a drone course. He's clear that the skill he picks may not outlast the five years. His partner's own night study is a quiet model for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do it fairly, and if we waste it that's on the people in charge. I'd want my union and my local member of parliament talking about it now, not in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be thirty-seven. I think I'd be okay if I'm not lazy about it. I could become the guy who fixes the machines, or move out of mining altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Years one and two I'd keep the loader job and get the remote ticket. Then the electrical apprenticeship, even if it means a pay cut for a while, which is scary with no savings. And Ana and I would probably wait on kids until we know where we land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It feels like something I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said waiting on kids. Was that something you'd planned sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about maybe in two or three years. Ana's thirty in March. She'd want me to say it's money and not the robots, and it is money, but the robots make the money question harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A pay cut for an apprenticeship with no savings. How would you actually manage that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd need the company or the government to top it up. Without that I'd have to do weekend work, maybe at my cousin's tyre shop. I don't love it, but tyres don't go anywhere fast.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly and if it's wasted that's on the people in charge. I'd want the union and my local member of parliament on it now.
S4.think: I think I'd be okay at thirty-seven if I'm not lazy about it. I could become the person who fixes the machines or leave mining altogether.
S4.do: Keeps the loader job and gets the remote ticket in the first two years, then starts an electrical apprenticeship despite the pay cut. Delays having children with his partner and plans weekend work at a cousin's tyre shop to bridge the gap.
S4.feel: Uneasy but okay, because it feels like something he can plan for.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he lays out a clear sequence and becomes almost hopeful. The cost shows up in family plans: he and his partner would hold off on children. He's honest that the apprenticeship only works with a wage top-up or extra weekend work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. With five or ten I can see steps, with two I can only see my mother's spare room. What would help is being paid while you retrain, like a wage, because nobody on my rate can stop earning for a year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the older guys. Everyone worries about young people, but I'll find something. Rafa's fifty-eight and all he knows is rock, and he's the best miner I've met.

headlineQuote: With five or ten I can see steps, with two I can only see my mother's spare room.
portrait: Pedro Lopez is a 27-year-old trainee loader operator on level 14 of an underground gold mine, living with his girlfriend Ana, a care worker, with almost nothing saved. He's a union man who uses AI chat apps now and then to get through manuals, and he likes to see what works before he moves. In the slow pictures he lines up a remote operator ticket and then an electrical apprenticeship. The two-year picture takes away that ladder and sends him back to his mother's house, and the ten-year one leads him and Ana to hold off on children.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he can see steps with five or ten years but only his mother's spare room with two.
whatWouldHelp: Being paid a wage while he retrains, because nobody on a trainee's rate can stop earning for a year.
